name: Exploring Colleges, Careers, Trades, and the Military
title: Exploring Colleges, Careers, Trades, and the Military
answer: This idea is that college and career exploration should cover four year colleges, trade programs, apprenticeships, community colleges, and military service, with every path treated with respect. It matters because students need accurate information and balanced options that fit their interests, finances, and goals, and because career and technical students increasingly need practical AI skills. The student keeps the decision about where to apply.

sections.body: The idea addresses the narrow assumption that every student is heading to a four year college. It asks counselors and teachers to help students explore colleges, trades, apprenticeships, community colleges, and military service as legitimate routes to good careers. Tools such as BigFuture and Scoir can help students search by major, location, cost, and other factors, and counselors can help build balanced lists. A balanced list includes schools where a student is likely to be admitted and can afford to attend. The student chooses where to apply, so the exploration supports choice rather than replacing it.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In middle school, interest inventories and career profiles in tools such as Scoir and BigFuture can help students connect their interests to possible careers, and teachers can build lessons around careers related to their subjects. This early exploration helps students make better choices when high school course selection arrives. In high school, counselors can help students build balanced college lists and can use official sources, such as military recruitment sites and state workforce agencies, to give accurate information about trades, apprenticeships, community colleges, and military service. For students in career and technical programs, practical AI skills are becoming part of the job, and the text notes that apprentices and their teachers wanted training in basic AI concepts taught through hands on, practical activities. AI tools can help organize this information, but details should always come from official sources.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text reports one study finding: a study in Germany found that apprentices and their teachers wanted training in basic AI concepts taught through hands on, practical activities (Rott et al., 2022). The rest of the idea rests on practice and on the use of official sources rather than on a body of research presented in the text. The supplied text does not state an evidence label for this idea.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets limits on how AI fits into this work. AI tools can help organize information, but details should always come from official sources, such as military recruitment sites and state workforce agencies. Counselors can help build balanced lists, but the student chooses where to apply. The text also warns against treating a four year college as the only respectable path, since trade programs, apprenticeships, community colleges, and military service all lead to good careers. The decisions about which path to explore and where to apply stay with the student, not with an AI tool.
